flashcard_questions.q: What is meant by background radiation?
flashcard_questions.a: Low-level radiation all around us from natural and artificial sources.

flashcard_questions.q: What proportion of background radiation comes from natural sources?
Which gas is the largest single source of background radiation in the UK?
Which type of radiation does radon gas emit?
Which isotope is the most widely used medical tracer?
What is the half-life of technetium-99m?
Why must a medical tracer emit gamma or beta radiation?
flashcard_questions.a: Alpha would be absorbed before it could leave the body.

flashcard_questions.q: Which type of radiation is used to monitor the thickness of paper?
Which type of radiation is used to sterilise medical equipment?
What happens to a nucleus during nuclear fission?
flashcard_questions.a: A large unstable nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei, releasing energy.

flashcard_questions.q: What is fired at a uranium-235 nucleus to induce fission?
What is the job of the control rods in a nuclear reactor?
flashcard_questions.a: They absorb neutrons to control the rate of the chain reaction.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the job of the moderator in a nuclear reactor?
flashcard_questions.a: It slows down the fast-moving neutrons released by fission.

flashcard_questions.q: What happens to nuclei during nuclear fusion?
flashcard_questions.a: Two small light nuclei join to form a larger, heavier nucleus.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is nuclear fusion so difficult to achieve on Earth?
flashcard_questions.a: Positively charged nuclei repel, so temperatures of millions of degrees are needed.

notes: 15 cards: 4 term to definition, 3 structure to function (control rods, moderator, tracer), 3 radiation-choice cards (alpha, beta, gamma), 2 value cards (85%, 6-hour half-life), 3 why/what-happens-if.
